16.0.0.en: The believers in the Church of Jerusalem were in need of help, so St. Paul instructs the Church of Corinth, as he had previously instructed the Church of Galatia, to gather contributions to supply the needs of the poor of Jerusalem.

16.1.0.en: St. Paul asks them that each of them who is able should be diligent to lay aside on the first day of the week, that is, Sunday, the amount his means allow, so that no time is lost in collecting when he comes to them.

16.1.1.en: This shows that giving took place on Sunday, the Lord’s Day, when they prayed the Liturgies.

16.2.0.en: When I come to you, choose from among those you trust representatives of yours to carry your gift, sent with letters from me to Jerusalem; and I am ready to accompany the representatives if what they have collected is large and needs greater care in delivering it.

16.2.1.en: The Church is one in every place, so do not withhold your feeling for your needy brethren in any church other than your own, but help as much as you can, not only with money but with all the help you are able to give. And care for the poor, because Christ called him His brother, so you offer love to Christ Himself when you help someone in need.

16.3.0.en: I will come to you after I pass through Macedonia, for I have decided to pass through it first.

16.4.0.en: According to some scholars, St. Paul wrote his Epistle to the Corinthians at the Passover of the year A.D. 57, which means that the winter the Apostle would spend in Corinth was the winter of A.D. 57-58.

16.5.0.en: St. Paul planned to visit Corinth so that it would not be a mere temporary passing through to another place; he wanted to stay with them a sufficient time and not be content with merely passing by them, perhaps because of the many problems that were among them. But here he puts the Lord’s will first because he knows that the Lord arranges his missionary journeys.

16.5.1.en: This is an example for us to put the Lord’s will before our own will, and to know that it is He who arranges all our affairs according to His will.

16.5.2.en: The First Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Corinthians

16.6.0.en: But I will tarry at Ephesus until Pentecost, which is the feast of the descent of the Holy Spirit and comes fifty days after the feast of the Resurrection.

16.6.1.en: From this we learn that he wrote this Epistle at Ephesus, and the time of its writing was before the day of Pentecost.

16.7.0.en: The Apostle refers to the success he had met with in preaching, and how his ministry brought great results and good fruits. Yet this success stirred up the wicked against him.

16.7.1.en: The presence of problems in the ministry does not lead to despair; rather it may be a sign that the ministry is effective and that Satan has been moved to oppose it. So let us continue in our striving and likewise in our spiritual life, and if we fall let us not be disturbed but resist the devil and he will flee from us, and in the end God prepares for us many blessings and crowns.

16.8.0.en: Timothy was in Macedonia at that time and was on his way, as the Apostle had ordered him, to Corinth at the arrival of this Epistle to its people. So the Apostle asked them to support him against the false teachers who stir up some people against him, because Timothy does the work that the Lord commanded, that is, preaching, as Paul does.

16.9.0.en: St. Paul instructed them not to despise him for his youth, that he might return to him in peace with his companions after completing the work for which he sent him.

16.10.0.en: In spite of Paul’s encouragements to Apollos, he did not wish to come now to Corinth, that is, up to the writing of this Epistle, but he promised to do so when he sees that the time is suitable. Perhaps this was to avoid the quarrels between the parties that had formed in Corinth, where one says, I am of Paul, and another, I am of Apollos. So he wanted to delay his visit until matters calm down and the quarrels disappear.

16.11.0.en: In this verse are four commands suited to the circumstances of the Church of Corinth:

16.11.1.en: The first: “Watch ye”: the Church must always watch so as to be alert to the attacks of the enemy of good, and be warned of the evils mentioned in this Epistle, which are factions, quarrels, misconduct, and false teachers.

16.11.2.en: The second: “Stand fast in the faith”: that is, to stand firm in the truth that they heard from him and accepted and confessed, and especially to hold fast to the doctrine of the resurrection, which some had denied.

16.11.3.en: The third: “Quit you like men”: that is, to be courageous in standing firm before the enemies of the truth, to refute the arguments of the Jewish scholars and the philosophers of the Gentiles.

16.11.4.en: The fourth: “Be strong”: to endure hardships and persecutions.

16.12.0.en: He asks them that love possess their hearts and be the foundation of all their conduct in their homes and their spiritual gatherings.

16.12.1.en: The First Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Corinthians. The need of the Church of Corinth for this advice is evident from what was reported of the news of quarrels and what happens among them even in partaking of the Lord’s Supper. St. Paul elaborated on the subject of love in chapter thirteen.

16.13.0.en: Achaia: the southern region of Greece.

16.13.1.en: The saints: that is, the believers.

16.13.2.en: The Apostle refers to the house of Stephanas, which was distinguished as a whole family that had consecrated itself to the Lord. By the word firstfruits he means that the house of Stephanas was the first of the families to show the life of true faith that bears fruit in service to others.

16.14.0.en: St. Paul instructs them to cooperate with these and with whoever serves with them and labors in the Lord’s vineyard.

16.14.1.en: We find a similar commandment in the Epistle to the Hebrews, where the Apostle says, “Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls” (Heb 13:17).

16.15.0.en: The coming of Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus from Corinth to Ephesus, where the Apostle was, was a comfort to him because of his distance from the people of Corinth. They eased somewhat his longing and anxiety for them.

16.16.0.en: The good news these men brought relieved the Apostle’s soul and filled his heart with reassurance, and he also expects that through this Epistle which the Apostle will send them, they too will feel peace of mind.

16.16.1.en: He then instructs them to honor these servants and recognize their worth.

16.16.2.en: May we honor those who serve us, so that their service to us may be with joy and we may benefit from it to the utmost, because by this we honor Christ, of whom they are an image.

16.16.3.en: And as we humble ourselves we learn more from them and receive more abundant blessings from God, so that the ministry grows and many souls find rest in Christ.

16.17.0.en: Aquila and Priscilla: a man and his wife who believed at the hand of Paul in Corinth and served with him; their trade was the same as Paul’s, which was tentmaking, so he worked it with them to provide for his needs, and they accompanied him on his missionary journeys.

16.17.1.en: Christians are bound together by a spiritual bond, and by virtue of this bond they feel their unity in Christ and convey greetings of love to one another. This is what the Christians in Asia (present-day Turkey) did with the people of Corinth.

16.17.2.en: It appears from this verse that the house of Aquila and Priscilla was used as a church for the believers, since it was not easy to establish churches because of the many persecutions.

16.18.0.en: All the brethren send their greetings.

16.18.1.en: “Greet ye one another with an holy kiss”: this same expression is proclaimed by the deacon to the congregation of worshippers in the Divine Liturgy, and this holy kiss embodies the love latent in the hearts of the believers for one another.

16.18.2.en: The First Epistle of Paul the Apostle to the Corinthians

16.19.0.en: “The salutation of me Paul with mine own hand”: this means that he wrote this phrase with his own hand, although the weakness of his sight made him dictate his letters to another. This phrase also confirms that the Epistle is authentic and was written by St. Paul.

16.20.0.en: The Apostle considered the love of Christ to be the most important quality that distinguishes the Christian, and judged that its absence is the greatest of sins, and he condemns whoever is not characterized by it.

16.20.1.en: Anathema: a Greek word meaning delivered up to destruction.

16.20.2.en: Maranatha: its meaning is, The Lord is coming.

16.20.3.en: Let us look for the coming of the Lord with longing, and beware of falling into sins.

16.21.0.en: St. Paul asks that the grace of the Lord Jesus be with the Corinthians. This petition of the Apostle includes every temporal and eternal blessing.

16.22.0.en: By saying to them “my love be with you all,” he wanted the Corinthians to be sure of the intensity of his love and sincerity toward them, although he was compelled to rebuke them for some of their deeds, because his love for them is in Christ Jesus. Thus it is his duty to alert them to everything that could turn them aside from His way. Amen: its meaning is, May God confirm what I have said in this Epistle. When the Church says this word, it means an acknowledgment of the truth of the teachings declared, and that these teachings are the subject of their faith and hope.

16.22.1.en: The best thing you can offer to others is your love, which appears not only in a material form but first in kind words and care for their feelings, so that they see Christ in you and are reassured, and recover their peace in the midst of the afflictions of life.
